abstract: |
  This note sets out the notation of a linear structural equation model with
  a mean structure and describes two non-iterative, equation-by-equation
  estimators as implemented in lavaan: model-implied instrumental-variable
  two-stage least squares (MIIV-2SLS) and the scaling and aggregated
  James–Stein estimators.
  For both procedures we state the estimators of the directed coefficients,
  the subsequent estimation of the variance, covariance, and mean-structure
  parameters, and the default coefficient covariance estimators. For the
  James–Stein estimator we write the complete estimation procedure as a map
  from the sample moments to the parameter estimates and give the resulting
  delta-method standard errors.

# Model, Notation, and Parameterization

Consider a linear structural equation model for independent and identically
distributed observations $i=1,\ldots,n$. Following the all-y LISREL notation 
(Jöreskog & Sörbom, 1996, submodel 3B, Chapter 6; Rosseel & Vidal, 2025), let $\mathbf{y}_i\in\mathbb{R}^p$
contain the observed variables and $\boldsymbol{\eta}_i\in\mathbb{R}^q$ the
latent variables. The measurement and latent variable models are

$$
\mathbf{y}_i
=
\boldsymbol{\nu}+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\eta}_i
+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\eta}_i
=
\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\eta}_i
+\boldsymbol{\zeta}_i,
$$ {#eq-model}
where $\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ contains the measurement intercepts,
$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}$ contains the factor loadings,
$\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^q$ contains the latent variable intercepts,
and $\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q}$ contains the latent regression
coefficients, that is, the regression coefficients among the latent
variables. The measurement errors
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i\in\mathbb{R}^p$ and latent variable disturbances
$\boldsymbol{\zeta}_i\in\mathbb{R}^q$ have zero means. 
Let $\mathbb{S}_+^k$ and $\mathbb{S}_{++}^k$ denote the sets of symmetric
positive semidefinite and positive definite $k\times k$ matrices,
respectively. Assume
$\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i)=\boldsymbol{\Theta}\in\mathbb{S}_+^p$,
$\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\zeta}_i)=\boldsymbol{\Psi}\in\mathbb{S}_+^q$,
and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i,\boldsymbol{\zeta}_i)=\mathbf{0}_{p\times q}$.

Provided that $\mathbf{I}_q-\mathbf{B}$ is nonsingular, the latent and
observed mean vectors are

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_\eta
=
(\mathbf{I}_q-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\alpha}
\in\mathbb{R}^q,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\mu}_y
=
\boldsymbol{\nu}+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\mu}_\eta
\in\mathbb{R}^p,
$$ {#eq-means}
where $\mathbf{I}_q$ is the $q\times q$ identity matrix. The implied
observed covariance matrix is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
=
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\mathbf{I}_q-\mathbf{B})^{-1}
\boldsymbol{\Psi}
(\mathbf{I}_q-\mathbf{B})^{-\top}
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\top}
+
\boldsymbol{\Theta}.
$$ {#eq-sigma}

Both estimation procedures considered here require a marker
parameterization, in which one loading per factor is fixed to one and the
corresponding measurement intercept is fixed to zero. Collecting the marker
indicators gives
$\mathbf{m}_i=\boldsymbol{\eta}_i+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i^{(m)}$, where
$\mathbf{m}_i,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i^{(m)}\in\mathbb{R}^q$.

Let $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ collect the free
parameters, where $\mathcal{T}$ incorporates identification restrictions and
covariance admissibility conditions. Assume that
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^p$. Denote the
sample mean vector and covariance matrix by
$\overline{\mathbf{y}}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ and $\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{S}_+^p$,
respectively. Define

$$
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\overline{\mathbf{y}}\\
\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf{S})
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^h,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\mu}_y(\boldsymbol{\theta})\\
\operatorname{vech}\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\}
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^h,
\qquad
h=p+\frac{p(p+1)}{2},
$$ {#eq-moments}
where $\operatorname{vech}$ stacks the lower-triangular entries, including
the diagonal.

# Estimation of Factor Loadings and Latent Regression Coefficients

Model-implied instrumental-variable estimation [@bollen_1996;
@bollen_2018] and James–Stein estimation [@burghgraeve_etall_2021] obtain
factor loadings and latent regression coefficients equation by
equation. These coefficients are estimated from centered observations, with
intercepts estimated subsequently. The following expressions concern
unconstrained coefficients.

## Model-Implied Instrumental-Variable Estimation

In model-implied instrumental-variable (MIIV) estimation [@bollen_1996], the
marker equations are rearranged as

$$
\boldsymbol{\eta}_i
=
\mathbf{m}_i-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i^{(m)}
$$ {#eq-miiv-substitution}
and substituted into the remaining measurement and latent variable
equations. This produces equations involving observed responses and
regressors, with composite errors containing the original disturbances and
marker measurement errors.

After centering and stacking observations, equation $j$ has the
representation

$$
\mathbf{d}_j
=
\mathbf{X}_j\mathbf{a}_j+\mathbf{u}_j,
$$ {#eq-miiv-equation}
where $\mathbf{d}_j\in\mathbb{R}^n$ contains the $n$ centered observations
of the dependent variable of equation $j$, which is an indicator for a
measurement equation and the marker of the dependent latent variable for a
latent variable equation, $\mathbf{X}_j\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_j}$ contains
the centered observations of the markers of the $k_j$ latent predictors,
$\mathbf{a}_j\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$ contains the corresponding factor loadings
or latent regression coefficients, and $\mathbf{u}_j\in\mathbb{R}^n$ contains
the composite errors. The regressors
correlate with the composite errors because both contain the marker
measurement errors.

The hypothesized model identifies observed variables that are uncorrelated
with the composite error and sufficiently related to the regressors
[@bollen_1996; @bollen_2018]. Let
$\mathbf{Z}_j\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times\ell_j}$ contain these centered
instruments, with $\ell_j\geq k_j$. The MIIV two-stage least-squares
estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{j,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
(\mathbf{X}_j^{\top}\mathbf{P}_j\mathbf{X}_j)^{-1}
\mathbf{X}_j^{\top}\mathbf{P}_j\mathbf{d}_j,
\qquad
\mathbf{P}_j
=
\mathbf{Z}_j
(\mathbf{Z}_j^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_j)^{-1}
\mathbf{Z}_j^{\top}
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.
$$ {#eq-miiv-estimator}

## James–Stein Estimation

The James–Stein approach replaces the latent predictors in each equation by
estimates of their conditional expectations given observed proxies, followed
by least squares [@burghgraeve_etall_2021]. The least-squares step requires
the error of each equation to be uncorrelated with its latent predictors and with the measurement
errors of the proxies. In the scaling version, the proxies are the marker
indicators.

Let $\mathcal{P}_j$ index the $k_j$ latent predictors of equation $j$. The
corresponding marker equations are

$$
\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
=
\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
+
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(m)}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j},
$$ {#eq-marker}
where all three vectors belong to $\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$. Define

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{mm,j}
=
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j})
\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{k_j},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j
=
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(m)}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j})
\in\mathbb{S}_+^{k_j}.
$$ {#eq-marker-var}

Under joint normality,

$$
E(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}\mid\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j})
=
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}
+
\mathbf{R}_j
\left(
\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
-
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}
\right),
$$ {#eq-condexp}
where $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$ and

$$
\mathbf{R}_j
=
(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{mm,j}-\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j)
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{mm,j}^{-1}
\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j\times k_j}.
$$ {#eq-reliability}

Without normality, the same expression gives the best linear predictor under
the stated covariance assumptions [@burghgraeve_etall_2021]. The reliability adjustment $\mathbf{R}_j$
is not a covariance matrix and need not be symmetric.

Preliminary measurement-error variances are obtained using a Spearman-type
procedure [@burghgraeve_etall_2021; @lavaan_estimator_js]. Incorporating the small-sample correction gives

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_j
=
\left(
\mathbf{S}_{mm,j}
-
c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j
\right)
\mathbf{S}_{mm,j}^{-1},
\qquad
c_n=\frac{n-3}{n-1},
$$ {#eq-reliability-hat}
where $n>3$, $\mathbf{S}_{mm,j}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{k_j}$ is the sample
covariance matrix of the markers, and
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j\in\mathbb{S}_+^{k_j}$ contains their
preliminary measurement error covariance estimates, which are diagonal when
the marker errors are uncorrelated. These preliminary estimates provide the
reliability adjustment and are distinct from the final model variance
estimates described below.

Using the marker sample means
$\overline{\mathbf{m}}_{\mathcal{P}_j}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$, the fitted latent
predictors are

$$
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
=
\overline{\mathbf{m}}_{\mathcal{P}_j}
+
\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_j
\left(
\mathbf{m}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
-
\overline{\mathbf{m}}_{\mathcal{P}_j}
\right)
\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}.
$$ {#eq-fitted-eta}

Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_j\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_j}$ contain these fitted
predictors after centering. The coefficient estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{j,\mathrm{JS}}
=
(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_j^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_j)^{-1}
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_j^{\top}\mathbf{d}_j.
$$ {#eq-js-estimator}

## Aggregated James–Stein Estimation

The aggregated James–Stein estimator uses weighted aggregates of eligible
indicators as proxies, where an indicator is eligible for an equation when
its measurement error is uncorrelated with the error of that equation. For
latent predictor $k$ in equation $j$, let
$\mathbf{y}_{i,kj}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{kj}}$ contain the eligible indicators,
with corresponding intercepts $\boldsymbol{\nu}_{kj}$, loadings
$\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{kj}$, and weights $\mathbf{w}_{kj}$, all in
$\mathbb{R}^{r_{kj}}$. The response indicator is excluded from its own
predictor aggregate.

Normalize the aggregate to the factor's marker scale:

$$
a_{ikj}
=
\frac{
\mathbf{w}_{kj}^{\top}
(\mathbf{y}_{i,kj}-\boldsymbol{\nu}_{kj})
}{
\mathbf{w}_{kj}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{kj}
}
=
\eta_{ik}+\varepsilon^{(A)}_{ikj},
\qquad
\mathbf{w}_{kj}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{kj}\neq0.
$$ {#eq-aggregate}

The weights are chosen to maximize reliability [@bentler_1968]. In the
sample, they are estimated from indicator covariances and preliminary
measurement-error variances, and preliminary loading estimates from the
scaling procedure supply the normalization.

Collect the aggregates and their measurement errors in

$$
\mathbf{a}_{ij}
=
(a_{ikj})_{k\in\mathcal{P}_j}
\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(A)}_{ij}
=
(\varepsilon^{(A)}_{ikj})_{k\in\mathcal{P}_j}
\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}.
$$ {#eq-agg-vectors}

Let

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa,j}
=
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{a}_{ij})
\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{k_j},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{A,j}
=
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(A)}_{ij})
\in\mathbb{S}_+^{k_j}.
$$ {#eq-agg-var}

The corresponding conditional-expectation expression is

$$
E(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}\mid\mathbf{a}_{ij})
=
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}
+
\mathbf{R}_{A,j}
(\mathbf{a}_{ij}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\eta,\mathcal{P}_j}),
\qquad
\mathbf{R}_{A,j}
=
(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa,j}-\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{A,j})
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa,j}^{-1}.
$$ {#eq-agg-condexp}

As in the scaling version, this is an exact conditional expectation under
joint normality and otherwise a best linear predictor.

Because coefficient estimation uses centered observations, the empirical
aggregates can be calculated without first estimating intercepts:

$$
\widehat{a}^{\,c}_{ikj}
=
\frac{
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}^{\top}
(\mathbf{y}_{i,kj}-\overline{\mathbf{y}}_{kj})
}{
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}^{\top}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kj}
}.
$$ {#eq-agg-centered}

Let $\widehat{\mathbf{a}}^{\,c}_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_j}$ collect these
centered aggregates, and let $\mathbf{S}_{aa,j}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{k_j}$
denote their sample covariance matrix. The corresponding aggregate-error
covariance estimate has entries

$$
[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{A,j}]_{kl}
=
\frac{
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}^{\top}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kl,j}
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{lj}
}{
\left(
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{kj}^{\top}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kj}
\right)
\left(
\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{lj}^{\top}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{lj}
\right)
},
\qquad
k,l\in\mathcal{P}_j,
$$ {#eq-agg-omega}
where $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^{\,\mathrm{pre}}_{kl,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{kj}\times r_{lj}}$
contains the preliminary measurement-error covariances between the eligible
indicators of predictors $k$ and $l$. The matrix is diagonal when
measurement errors are uncorrelated.

The estimated reliability adjustment and centered fitted predictors are

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{A,j}
=
(\mathbf{S}_{aa,j}-c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{A,j})
\mathbf{S}_{aa,j}^{-1},
\qquad
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{\,c,A}_{i,\mathcal{P}_j}
=
\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{A,j}\widehat{\mathbf{a}}^{\,c}_{ij}.
$$ {#eq-agg-fitted}

Collecting the fitted predictors in
$\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_j}$ gives

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{j,\mathrm{JSA}}
=
(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A,j}^{\top}
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A,j})^{-1}
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A,j}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_j.
$$ {#eq-jsa-estimator}

# Estimation of Variance, Covariance, and Intercept Parameters

After estimating the factor loadings and latent regression coefficients,
the remaining variance and covariance parameters are obtained through a
separate covariance-fitting step. The completion procedure described here uses
reweighted least squares [@maydeuolivares_etall_2026]. Let

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{H}}
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}
(\mathbf{I}_q-\widehat{\mathbf{B}})^{-1}
\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q},
$$ {#eq-H}
where $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}$ and $\widehat{\mathbf{B}}$ are
obtained using the selected coefficient estimator. Conditional on these
estimates, the implied covariance matrix is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{v})
=
\widehat{\mathbf{H}}\boldsymbol{\Psi}(\mathbf{v})
\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}
+
\boldsymbol{\Theta}(\mathbf{v}),
$$ {#eq-sigma-v}
where $\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v}$ collects the free variance and
covariance parameters.

With fixed entries and linear equality restrictions incorporated into the
parameterization,

$$
\operatorname{vech}\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{v})\}
=
\widehat{\mathbf{c}}+\widehat{\mathbf{G}}\mathbf{v},
$$ {#eq-vech-linear}
where $t=p(p+1)/2$, $\widehat{\mathbf{c}}\in\mathbb{R}^t$ contains the
contributions of fixed parameters, and
$\widehat{\mathbf{G}}\in\mathbb{R}^{t\times d_v}$ maps the free parameters to
the implied covariance moments.

For a weight matrix $\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^t$, the weighted
least-squares estimate is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{v}}
=
\left(
\widehat{\mathbf{G}}^{\top}
\widehat{\mathbf{W}}
\widehat{\mathbf{G}}
\right)^{-1}
\widehat{\mathbf{G}}^{\top}
\widehat{\mathbf{W}}
\left\{
\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf{S})-\widehat{\mathbf{c}}
\right\},
$$ {#eq-wls-v}
assuming that $\widehat{\mathbf{G}}$ has full column rank.

Reweighted least squares updates the normal-theory weight matrix
[@browne_1974] using the current implied covariance matrix:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{W}}^{(r)}
=
\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{D}_p^{\top}
\left[
\{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(r)}\}^{-1}
\otimes
\{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(r)}\}^{-1}
\right]\mathbf{D}_p,
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(r)}
=
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\widehat{\mathbf{v}}^{(r)}).
$$ {#eq-rls-weights}

Here, $\otimes$ denotes the Kronecker product, and
$\mathbf{D}_p\in\mathbb{R}^{p^2\times t}$ is the duplication matrix
satisfying
$\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{S})=\mathbf{D}_p\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf{S})$.
Starting from an initial estimate with a positive definite implied
covariance matrix, the weighted least-squares update is repeated until
convergence. The resulting $\widehat{\mathbf{v}}$ determines
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}$ and $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}$.

Although the population covariance matrices must be positive semidefinite,
the unconstrained estimates need not satisfy this condition. Imposing
covariance admissibility constraints would require a constrained estimation
procedure.

Under the marker parameterization, if all nonmarker measurement intercepts
and all latent-variable intercepts are freely estimated, the mean structure
is saturated. Let $\overline{\mathbf{m}}\in\mathbb{R}^q$ contain the sample
marker means. Then

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_\eta
=
\overline{\mathbf{m}},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
=
\overline{\mathbf{y}}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}\overline{\mathbf{m}}
\in\mathbb{R}^p,
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
=
(\mathbf{I}_q-\widehat{\mathbf{B}})
\overline{\mathbf{m}}
\in\mathbb{R}^q.
$$ {#eq-mean-estimates}

These expressions preserve the fixed zero marker intercepts and reproduce
the observed sample means. Additional mean-structure restrictions require a
corresponding constrained estimation step. Together, these stages estimate the 
free entries of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$,
$\boldsymbol{\Psi}$, $\boldsymbol{\nu}$, and $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$. 

# Analytical Standard Errors

For MIIV coefficient estimates, the conventional homoskedastic covariance
estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{j,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
\widehat{\sigma}_{u_j}^{\,2}
(\mathbf{X}_j^{\top}\mathbf{P}_j\mathbf{X}_j)^{-1}
\in\mathbb{S}_+^{k_j},
$$ {#eq-miiv-vcov}
where

$$
\widehat{\sigma}_{u_j}^{\,2}
=
\frac{\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_j^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_j}
{n-k_j-1},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_j
=
\mathbf{d}_j-\mathbf{X}_j\widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{j,\mathrm{MIIV}},
$$ {#eq-miiv-sigma2}
for an equation with an estimated intercept and $n>k_j+1$. The variance
$\sigma_{u_j}^{2}$ concerns the transformed equation's composite error. It is
generally not an individual measurement-error or latent-variable
disturbance variance.

@burghgraeve_etall_2021 used bootstrap standard errors for James–Stein
estimation. Analytical standard errors can instead be obtained by
differentiating the complete estimation procedure with respect to the sample
moments.

For $T\in\{\mathrm{JS},\mathrm{JSA}\}$, write

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_T=g_{n,T}(\mathbf{s}),
$$ {#eq-js-map}
where $g_{n,T}$ maps the $h$ sample moments to the $d$ parameter estimates.
This mapping includes the preliminary error-variance estimates, coefficient
estimates, subsequent covariance estimates, and intercept estimates.

Suppose

$$
\sqrt{n}\{
\mathbf{s}-\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
\}
\xrightarrow{d}
N_h(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Gamma}),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\in\mathbb{S}_+^h,
$$ {#eq-clt}
where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is the joint asymptotic covariance matrix of the
sample means and covariances. Under the required moment and
differentiability conditions, the delta-method covariance estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_T
=
\frac{1}{n}
\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_T
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}
\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_T^{\top}
\in\mathbb{S}_+^d,
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_T
=
\left.
\frac{\partial g_{n,T}(\mathbf{s})}
{\partial\mathbf{s}^{\top}}
\right|_{\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{obs}}}
\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times h}.
$$ {#eq-js-vcov}

The Jacobian propagates uncertainty through all stimation stages. For
aggregated James–Stein estimation, this includes the estimated aggregation
weights and normalization loadings. It also includes the dependence of the
final variance, covariance, and intercept estimates on the estimated
directed coefficients.

The matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ may be estimated under multivariate
normality or using empirical moments through order four [@browne_1984]. For parameter
$r=1,\ldots,d$, the analytical standard error is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat{\theta}_{T,r})
=
\sqrt{[\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_T]_{rr}}
\in[0,\infty).
$$ {#eq-js-se}

The same delta-method construction can be applied to the complete MIIV
estimation map when moment-based standard errors are used. It is a distinct
covariance construction from the conventional equation-specific MIIV
expression given above.

# Simulation

We consider the model in @fig-model, with three latent variables and eleven
indicators. The latent-variable model is
$\eta_{2}=\alpha_2+b_1\eta_{1}+\zeta_{2}$ and
$\eta_{3}=\alpha_3+b_2\eta_{1}+b_3\eta_{2}+\zeta_{3}$, so that $b_1$, $b_2$,
and $b_3$ are the free elements of $\mathbf{B}$. Data are generated under
multivariate normality from the population values given in the code below.
Two factors are varied: the sample size, $n\in\{50, 100, 200, 300, 400,
500\}$, and the reliability of the indicators, which is set to .6 or .8 for
every indicator by choosing the residual variances
$\theta_j=\lambda_j^2\operatorname{Var}(\eta_{k})(1-\rho)/\rho$, with $\rho$
the target reliability. This gives 12 conditions with 1,000 replications
each. Each data set is analyzed with the scaling and the aggregated
James–Stein estimators, the MIIV two-stage least-squares estimator, and
maximum likelihood, all with a mean structure.

The focus is on the standard errors. For every free parameter we compute the
empirical standard deviation of the estimates (efficiency), the ratio of the
mean estimated standard error to that empirical standard deviation, the
relative bias of the variance estimator, that is, the mean of the squared
standard errors divided by the empirical variance of the estimates, so that a
value of one indicates an unbiased variance estimator, and the coverage of the
95% confidence intervals. The relative bias and coverage are accompanied by
their Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE). @fig-sim-structural-60 and
@fig-sim-structural-80 show the results for the latent regression coefficients
$b_1$, $b_2$, and $b_3$ at reliability .6 and .8. @fig-sim-measurement-60 and
@fig-sim-measurement-80 summarize the results for the free factor loadings,
the residual variances of the indicators, and the variance of $\eta_1$
together with the disturbance variances, by showing for each class the mean
over its parameters and the range across them. The mean-structure parameters are not
compared because maximum likelihood uses a different parameterization of the
means by default. All analyses were conducted in R [@rcoreteam_2025] using the
lavaan package [@rosseel_2012] for estimation and the simhelpers package
[@joshi_pustejovsky_2025] for the performance criteria.

```{r}
#| label: simulation
#| cache: true
library(lavaan)
set.seed(1234)

lam <- c(1, 0.8, 1.2, 1, 0.9, 1.1, 1.0, 1, 0.9, 1.1, 1.0)
var_eta <- rep(c(1, 1, 1.02), c(3, 4, 4))   # Var(eta1), Var(eta2), Var(eta3)
pop_model <- function(rel) {
  theta <- lam^2 * var_eta * (1 - rel) / rel
  paste0('
  eta1 =~ 1*y1 + 0.8*y2 + 1.2*y3
  eta2 =~ 1*y4 + 0.9*y5 + 1.1*y6 + 1.0*y7
  eta3 =~ 1*y8 + 0.9*y9 + 1.1*y10 + 1.0*y11
  eta2 ~ 0.6*eta1
  eta3 ~ 0.3*eta1 + 0.5*eta2
  eta1 ~~ 1*eta1; eta2 ~~ 0.64*eta2; eta3 ~~ 0.5*eta3
  eta1 ~ 1*1; eta2 ~ 0.5*1; eta3 ~ 0.5*1
  y2 ~ 0.2*1; y3 ~ 0.2*1; y5 ~ 0.2*1; y6 ~ 0.2*1; y7 ~ 0.2*1
  y9 ~ 0.2*1; y10 ~ 0.2*1; y11 ~ 0.2*1
  ', paste0("y", 1:11, " ~~ ", round(theta, 4), "*y", 1:11, collapse = "; "))
}
mod <- '
  eta1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3
  eta2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6 + y7
  eta3 =~ y8 + y9 + y10 + y11
  eta2 ~ eta1
  eta3 ~ eta1 + eta2
'
ns <- c(50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500); rels <- c(0.6, 0.8); R <- 1000
cond <- expand.grid(n = ns, rel = rels)
est <- c("JS", "JSA", "IV", "ML")

one <- function(n, rel) {
  pop <- pop_model(rel)
  pt <- lavaanify(pop)
  true <- setNames(pt$ustart, paste0(pt$lhs, pt$op, pt$rhs))
  d <- simulateData(pop, sample.nobs = n)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(est, function(e) {
    fit <- try(sem(mod, data = d, estimator = e, meanstructure = TRUE),
               silent = TRUE)
    if (inherits(fit, "try-error") || !lavInspect(fit, "converged"))
      return(NULL)
    pe <- parameterEstimates(fit, remove.nonfree = TRUE)
    pe <- pe[pe$op != "~1", ]
    par <- paste0(pe$lhs, pe$op, pe$rhs)
    data.frame(n = n, rel = rel, estimator = e, par = par, true = true[par],
               est = pe$est, se = pe$se,
               ci.lower = pe$ci.lower, ci.upper = pe$ci.upper)
  }))
}
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cond)), function(i)
  do.call(rbind, replicate(R, one(cond$n[i], cond$rel[i]),
                           simplify = FALSE))))

```

```{r}
#| label: performance
library(simhelpers)
library(ggplot2)
summ <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(res, res[c("n", "rel", "estimator", "par")]),
  function(x) {
    tp <- x$true[1]
    ab <- calc_absolute(x, estimates = est, true_param = tp,
                        criteria = c("bias", "stddev"))
    rv <- calc_relative_var(x, estimates = est, var_estimates = se^2,
                            criteria = "relative bias")
    cv <- calc_coverage(x, lower_bound = ci.lower, upper_bound = ci.upper,
                        true_param = tp, criteria = "coverage")
    data.frame(x[1, c("n", "rel", "estimator", "par")],
               bias = ab$bias, sd = ab$stddev, se_sd = mean(x$se) / ab$stddev,
               rb_var = rv$rel_bias_var, rb_var_mcse = rv$rel_bias_var_mcse,
               coverage = cv$coverage, coverage_mcse = cv$coverage_mcse,
               reps = ab$K_absolute)
  }))
rownames(summ) <- NULL
summ$class <- ifelse(grepl("=~", summ$par), "Loadings",
               ifelse(grepl("~~", summ$par),
                      ifelse(grepl("^eta", summ$par), "Factor variances",
                             "Residual variances"), "Structural"))
summ$estimator <- factor(summ$estimator,
                         levels = c("JS", "JSA", "IV", "ML"))

## long format over the four criteria, with values above `cap` flagged
crit <- c(sd = "SD", se_sd = "SE/SD", rb_var = "RB(Var)",
          coverage = "Coverage")
mcse <- c(sd = NA, se_sd = NA, rb_var = "rb_var_mcse",
          coverage = "coverage_mcse")
cap <- 1.5
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(crit), function(k)
  data.frame(summ[c("n", "rel", "estimator", "par", "class")],
             criterion = crit[k],
             value = summ[[k]],
             mcse = if (is.na(mcse[k])) NA_real_ else summ[[mcse[k]]])))
long$criterion <- factor(long$criterion, levels = crit)
ref <- data.frame(criterion = factor(c("SE/SD", "RB(Var)", "Coverage"),
                                     levels = crit), y = c(1, 1, 0.95))
clip <- function(v) {
  i <- v$criterion %in% c("SE/SD", "RB(Var)")
  v$clipped <- i & v$value > cap
  v$value[v$clipped] <- cap
  if ("upper" %in% names(v)) {
    v$upper[i] <- pmin(v$upper[i], cap)
    v$lower[i] <- pmin(v$lower[i], cap)
    v$lower[v$clipped] <- v$upper[v$clipped] <- NA
  }
  v
}
pd <- position_dodge(width = 25)
plot_perf <- function(v, col, labeller = "label_value") {
  ggplot(v, aes(n, value, colour = estimator, shape = estimator,
                linetype = estimator)) +
    geom_hline(data = ref, aes(yintercept = y), colour = "grey55",
               linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0,
                  linetype = "solid", position = pd, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, position = pd) +
    geom_point(size = 2, position = pd) +
    geom_point(data = v[v$clipped, ], shape = 2, size = 3, position = pd,
               show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_grid(as.formula(paste("criterion ~", col)), scales = "free_y",
               switch = "y", labeller = labeller) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = ns) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(JS = "#2a78d6", JSA = "#eda100",
                                   IV = "#eb6834", ML = "#1baf7a")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(JS = 16, JSA = 18, IV = 15, ML = 17)) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(JS = "solid", JSA = "dashed",
                                     IV = "longdash", ML = "dotdash")) +
    labs(x = expression(italic(n)), y = NULL, colour = "Estimator",
         shape = "Estimator", linetype = "Estimator") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.placement = "outside",
          strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 90),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "grey80"))
}
plot_structural <- function(rel) {
  v <- long[long$class == "Structural" & long$rel == rel, ]
  v$par <- factor(v$par, levels = c("eta2~eta1", "eta3~eta1", "eta3~eta2"),
                  labels = c("b[1]", "b[2]", "b[3]"))
  v$lower <- v$value - v$mcse; v$upper <- v$value + v$mcse
  plot_perf(clip(v), "par", labeller = labeller(par = label_parsed))
}
plot_measurement <- function(rel) {
  w <- long[long$class != "Structural" & long$rel == rel, ]
  v <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
    split(w, w[c("n", "estimator", "class", "criterion")]),
    function(x) data.frame(x[1, c("n", "estimator", "class", "criterion")],
                           value = mean(x$value), lower = min(x$value),
                           upper = max(x$value))))
  v$class <- factor(v$class, levels = c("Loadings", "Residual variances",
                                        "Factor variances"))
  plot_perf(clip(v), "class")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-structural-60
#| fig-cap: "Performance of the standard errors of the latent regression coefficients at reliability .6, by estimator and sample size."
#| apa-note: "NoNote *Note.* JS denotes the scaling James–Stein estimator, JSA the aggregated James–Stein estimator, IV the MIIV two-stage least-squares estimator, and ML maximum likelihood. SD is the empirical standard deviation of the estimates, SE/SD the mean estimated standard error divided by SD, and RB(Var) the relative bias of the variance estimator, that is, the mean squared standard error divided by the empirical variance. Dotted lines mark the reference values of 1 for SE/SD and RB(Var) and .95 for coverage. Values of SE/SD and RB(Var) above 1.5 are drawn at 1.5 with an open triangle. Error bars for RB(Var) and coverage represent Monte Carlo standard errors."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| out-width: "100%"
plot_structural(0.6)
```
